title: The Official Guidebook Nobody Tells You About
summary: The government publishes a free guide to living in Japan in 19 languages, compiled across ministries. Almost no study-abroad site points to it.
body_html:
Most of what you need to know about living in Japan is already written down, officially, for free, in your language. The document is called the Living and Working Guidebook, it is supervised by the Immigration Services Agency, and the study-abroad industry almost never mentions it.

Worth asking why. It is free, so nobody earns anything by sending you to it.

What it is

The guidebook was compiled following a 2018 cabinet-level decision on comprehensive measures for accepting and integrating foreign nationals, with the ministries and agencies working as one to assemble the basic information needed for foreign residents in Japan to live and work safely. [source:1]

That is an unusual provenance. It is not one ministry's pamphlet about its own remit — the list of collaborating bodies runs from the Cabinet Secretariat and the National Police Agency through to the Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare and the Ministry of the Environment. [source:1] Which is why it covers things no single agency's page would: rubbish collection and pension enrolment and bicycle rules, in one document.

Multilingual versions are published on the Support Portal for Foreign Nationals, in 19 languages including Easy Japanese. [source:1]

Easy Japanese is worth noticing. If your Japanese is at the stage where the normal version is too hard and your own language feels too distant from the terms you will actually encounter at a counter, that version exists precisely for the gap.

Check which edition you have

This is the one piece of housekeeping that matters, because a stale copy of a government guide is worse than no copy.

The current one is the 8th edition. [source:1] It updates the 7th edition to reflect the creation, revision and abolition of systems as at 1 August 2025, and was published in 2026. [source:1]

So the content has a date, and the date is stated. If a copy you downloaded from a third-party site does not say which edition it is, discard it and take the current one from the portal. Immigration rules have changed recently enough that an older edition will tell you things that are no longer true.

What is actually in it

The chapter numbering runs to chapter 12. [source:1] The ones a language-school student will open are these.

Chapter 1, entry and residence procedures. [source:1] Residence card issue, address notification, loss, return, renewal, change of status, permission to engage in activity outside your status, and the notifications you owe the regional immigration office. [source:1] This is the chapter that maps to almost every deadline you have.

Chapter 2, procedures at your municipal office. [source:1] The notifications you must file locally, and the My Number system. [source:1] The distinction between what you file at immigration and what you file at the ward office is the single most common confusion in a student's first month, and this chapter is the other half of it.

Chapter 6, medical care. [source:1] Medical institutions, medical insurance, and medicines. [source:1]

Chapter 8, tax. [source:1] Income tax. [source:1] Short, and relevant to anyone with a part-time job.

Chapter 9, transport. [source:1] Traffic rules and manners, driving licences, owning a vehicle including motorbikes, and what to do when a traffic accident happens. [source:1]

Chapter 10, emergencies and disasters. [source:1] Emergency phone calls, disasters, and evacuation. [source:1]

Chapter 11, housing. [source:1] Housing in Japan, and moving in. [source:1]

Chapter 12, rules and customs in daily life. [source:1] Daily-life rules, and infection prevention. [source:1]

Chapter 3 covers employment and labour, chapter 7 pensions and welfare. [source:1] Both matter less on day one and more at renewal time than students expect.

The honest limitation

There is no chapter on studying abroad.

Chapter 5 is called education, and it covers the Japanese education system, financial support for education costs, and Japanese-language learning. [source:1] That is the school system from the perspective of a resident family — not a guide to being a language-school student.

So the guidebook is written for foreign residents of Japan generally. You are one, which is why most of it applies to you. But your specific situation — attendance requirements, the work-hour cap, what a school's accreditation status means — is not its subject, and you will not find it addressed as such.

Two practical consequences. The guidebook is the right source for how Japan works and a poor source for how your residence status works. And nobody has indexed it for students, which is why a document this useful can sit in plain sight unread.

How to use it

  • Download the current edition in your language from the Support Portal, and check the edition number against the one above. [source:1]
  • Read chapter 1 and chapter 2 before you arrive, not after. [source:1] They are the deadlines.
  • Read chapter 10 in your first week, while you still have time to read calmly. [source:1] It is the chapter you will need when you have no time to read.
  • Keep it on your phone, not in a downloads folder on a laptop you left at home.
  • Treat it as the baseline and your school's guidance as the specifics. Where they conflict, the guidebook is the one with a publication date and the collaborating ministries behind it — but on your residence status, go to the agency's own procedure pages.

We have written up the chapters most relevant to students separately: emergency numbers and disasters from the emergencies chapter, health insurance from the medical chapter, daily-life rules from the housing and daily-life chapters, and bicycles and traffic from the transport chapter. For the residence-status side, start with reporting obligations.

The guidebook itself is linked below. Read the original rather than anyone's summary of it, including ours.

claims_without_sources: 「無料だから誰も紹介しない」—— 当方の推測であり、業界の実態調査に基づくものではない。問いの形で出し、断定していない。
「やさしい日本語版が、母語版と通常版の間の隙間を埋める」—— 冊子はやさしい日本語を含む19言語と述べているだけで、どの読者に向くかは書いていない。当方の助言。
協力府省庁の数 —— 冊子は府省庁一覧を掲げているが「17」という数字そのものは本文に現れない。数を自分で数えて断定することは避け、一覧の両端（内閣官房・環境省など）を挙げる形にした。本文には府省庁の数を一切書いていない。
全157ページという分量 —— pdfinfo で得た値であって冊子の本文に印字された数字ではないため、記事に書いていない。闸门も本文テキストからは核対できない。
「在留資格の仕組みについては出典として弱い」—— 冊子の自己記述ではなく、当方の評価。章構成（留学の章が無いこと）から導いている。
「第1章・第2章が締切の地図になる」「第10章を最初の週に読め」—— 読み方の助言であって冊子の指示ではない。
2024年末の在留外国人数（約376万人）—— 冊子のはじめにに記載があるが、学生に関係する数字ではないうえ、万単位の表記が闸门の照合形式と合わないため本文では使っていない。
